A batch is a group of things of the same kind that are made, collected, or handled together, at one time.

The key thought behind this word is: instead of doing things one by one, you do them as a group, all at once. That group is a batch.

Three things are always true about a batch:

1. The items are similar or of the same type.
You make a batch of cookies — not a batch of cookies and a random chair thrown in. The things in a batch belong together because they're the same kind of thing.

2. They are grouped together deliberately.
A batch isn't a random pile. Someone consciously decides: "These things go together." They are collected or produced as one defined set.

3. They are made or dealt with together, in one go.
This is the heart of the word. The items in a batch share the same "session" — the same baking session, the same production run, the same processing moment.

Imagine a baker. She puts 12 cookies in the oven at 9 AM. Those 12 cookies come out together. That is one batch. Then at 10 AM, she puts another 12 cookies in. That is a second batch.

Notice: she didn't bake 24 cookies all at once. She baked them in batches — one group at a time. This is the most natural, intuitive example of the word.

The word travels across many areas of life, always carrying the same core meaning:

In cooking and baking:
"I made three batches of muffins for the party." Each time you bake a set of muffins, that's one batch.

In manufacturing and production:
Factories make products in batches. A pharmaceutical company might manufacture 10,000 bottles of medicine together in one production run — that is one batch. If something goes wrong, they can trace exactly which batch was affected (this is why medicine bottles have a "batch number" on them).

In computing:
A "batch" of data or tasks means a set of items that are processed together by a computer in one operation, rather than one at a time or in real time. For example, a bank might process all of the day's transactions at midnight in one batch, rather than updating your account every single second.

In everyday life:
The word is used loosely and naturally for any group of similar things that arrive or are dealt with together:

  • "A batch of emails" — a bunch of emails that came in together.
  • "A batch of new students" — a group of students who joined the school at the same time.
  • "A batch of applications" — a set of job applications received in the same period.
  • "A fresh batch of problems" — a new set of issues to solve.
A Subtle But Important Quality: Batches Imply Repetition

When someone says "a batch," they naturally suggest that there are, or could be, other batches. It's not just one single, unique group — it's one of potentially many rounds.

This is different from saying "a group" or "a collection," which don't carry that sense of repetition. "A batch" tells you: this is one round of something that happens in rounds.

A batch can be tiny or enormous. A batch of two cookies is still a batch. A batch of a million car parts is still a batch. What matters is not how big the group is, but the fact that the items were made or handled together, as one defined set.

• "a fresh batch" — a newly made or newly arrived group. "There's a fresh batch of bread at the bakery."
  • "in batches" — doing something group by group rather than all at once. "We'll process the orders in batches."
  • "a batch of" — the standard way to use the word, followed by whatever the items are. "A batch of reports."
  • "batch number" — an identification number assigned to a particular batch during production, used for tracking.
  • "the first/second/next batch" — specifying which round or group you mean.
A batch is a defined group of similar things that are produced, processed, or handled together, in one session — one of potentially many such rounds.
